113.title: Ash Wednesday: dust
113.hook: ashes on the forehead and the words: remember you are dust (Genesis 3:19)
113.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday, Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and others go to church to receive a cross of ash on the forehead, with words recalling Genesis 3:19; Orthodox Christians begin Great Lent on Clean Monday instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epiphany: strangers from the east, a river, a wedding. Your line was the light is for everyone. Did an outsider show you something? Now the circle turns darker. Day one hundred thirteen.

One Wednesday in late winter or early spring, you might notice it on the train, at the office, in the grocery line. A dark smudge on someone's forehead. Sometimes it's a neat cross. Sometimes just a gray thumbprint. People who don't know lean over and say, hey, you've got something on your face. They know. They put it there on purpose, or rather, someone did, that morning or at lunch, in a church. A minister or priest dipped a thumb in ash, pressed it to their forehead, and said a few words from the third chapter of Genesis, words about dust. It's the strangest makeup of the year. Today's word is the day it happens.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, forty-six days before Easter. The ashes are usually made by burning the palm branches from last year's Palm Sunday, so the year's celebration becomes this year's dust. And the words, in many churches, echo what God says to Adam in Genesis. In the King James: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." That's blunt. You will die. Everyone in this room will. Ashes in the Bible meant grief and turning around: Job, at the end of his long argument with God, says he repents "in dust and ashes." But here's the part that changes it. Go back one chapter in Genesis, to how the first human was made. "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life." There's even a pun in Hebrew. The human is adam. The ground is adamah. Earthling, from the earth. So being dust isn't only bad news. It's what God picked up, and shaped, and breathed into. A psalm puts it tenderly: "he remembereth that we are dust." Not as a threat. As someone who knows how fragile you are. Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and Methodists keep Ash Wednesday, and more and more other churches do too. Orthodox Christians don't; their Great Lent begins on a Monday called Clean Monday, after an evening when people ask one another's forgiveness. The ash is a reminder in two directions: you are dust, and you are loved.
screen: `LAST YEAR'S PALMS, BURNED.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `ADAM FROM ADAMAH.` · then, large: `HE REMEMBERETH THAT WE ARE DUST.` · then: `DUST, AND BREATHED INTO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch the ground. If there's a plant nearby, press a finger into its soil. If you're outside, touch the earth. If neither, look closely at the back of your hand. Settle, and breathe. Remember that you are made of the same stuff as the ground. You won't be here forever. Let that be true without panicking. Then notice your breath going in and out. If you pray, you can remember the other half: breathed into, and loved. If you don't, simply hold both at once: fragile, and here. The bell holds the time.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, when many Christians receive ashes on the forehead and hear that they are dust. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Today, when you wash your face or your hands, remember both halves of it. Day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: Lent: forty days
114.hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, echoing Jesus in the desert
114.howItsDone: During Lent many Christians fast in some way, pray more and give to the poor; Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and often skip meat on Fridays, Orthodox Christians keep a strict fast through Great Lent, and many Protestants give up or take up one personal practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, and your line: dust, and loved. Did you remember both halves when you washed your hands? The ash opens a season. Today, what comes next. Day one hundred fourteen.

Every spring you hear it at work, at school, in group chats. So what are you giving up for Lent? Chocolate. Coffee. Social media. Swearing. One person gives up nothing and says they're giving up giving things up. It can sound like a second round of New Year's resolutions. But the season started somewhere much older and much harder. In the Gospels, right after his baptism, Jesus goes out into the wilderness alone, and stays there. The King James says, "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Hungry, alone, tested, in the desert. Today's word is the season Christians built around those forty days.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?` → `INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Lent. It comes from an old English word for spring, when the days lengthen. In Greek and Latin the season is simply called the fortieth. Forty is a number the Bible keeps returning to. Forty days of rain for Noah. Forty days for Moses on the mountain. Forty years for Israel in the wilderness. Forty days for Elijah walking to the mountain of God. And forty days for Jesus in the desert. It's the Bible's number for a long, testing, transforming stretch. Lent is traditionally made of three practices, and they come from Jesus's own teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. He doesn't say if you fast. He says when. Churches keep it differently. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and many skip meat on the Fridays of Lent. Orthodox Christians keep the strictest fast, traditionally no meat, dairy or eggs for the whole of Great Lent. Many Protestants choose something personal, or take something up instead: reading a Gospel, volunteering, calling someone each day. Some churches don't mark Lent at all. But here's the idea that runs through all of them. Giving something up isn't meant as a punishment. It's meant to make room. The hour you'd spend scrolling becomes an hour for prayer. The money you'd spend on coffee goes to someone who needs it. The hunger itself becomes a reminder of what you're really hungry for. Less, so there's room. That's why Christians call it a season of preparation. It clears space for Easter.
screen: `LENCTEN: SPRING.` · `FORTY: THE BIBLE'S TESTING NUMBER.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LESS, TO MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small Lenten thing. It doesn't have to be Lent right now. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what's taking up too much room in your days. A habit, a screen, a snack, a complaint you keep repeating. Choose one small thing to set down for a week. Or choose one thing to take up in its place. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, just notice what fills the space. The bell holds the time.
Lent. From the old English for spring. Forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter, echoing Jesus in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: less, so there's room. Today, start your small thing, and when you feel its absence, let the gap remind you what you made room for. Day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Palm Sunday and Holy Week
115.hook: branches in, a cross by Friday; the week the whole year turns on
115.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday many churches bless and hand out palm branches, walk in procession and read the Passion; through Holy Week Christians gather for services each day toward Easter, and many walk the Stations of the Cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lent, forty days, and your line: less, so there's room. How is your small thing going? Lent walks toward one week. Today, we arrive at it. Day one hundred fifteen.

Jerusalem, a few days before Passover. The city is packed with pilgrims, maybe several times its usual size, and Roman soldiers are watching the crowds. A man comes over the Mount of Olives riding a young donkey. Not a warhorse. A donkey. And the crowd goes wild. People pull off their cloaks and throw them on the road in front of him. Others cut branches from the trees. John's Gospel says they "Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord." It feels like a parade. It feels like the beginning of something. And by Friday of that same week, he'll be on a Roman cross. Today, the week that everything turns on.
screen: `PASSOVER, A PACKED CITY.` → `A DONKEY, NOT A WARHORSE.` → `BRANCHES AND CLOAKS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Palm Sunday and Holy Week. Start with the shout. Hosanna. It sounds like a word of praise, and it became one, but it began as a plea. It comes from Hebrew in Psalm 118: save, please. Save us now. The crowd is shouting praise and a prayer for rescue at the same time. And the donkey matters. The prophet Zechariah had pictured Jerusalem's king coming humble, riding on a donkey. Jesus seems to choose that picture on purpose: a king, but not the kind with an army. Then the week unfolds. In the Gospels, Jesus clears the traders out of the temple. He teaches in its courts. A woman anoints him with costly perfume. On Thursday, a last supper with his friends. On Friday, the cross. On Saturday, silence. On Sunday, the empty tomb. People have long noticed how fast it turns, from palms to a cross in five days. Sometimes they say the same crowd that shouted hosanna shouted crucify, but the Gospels don't say that; they don't say who was in either crowd. Christians keep this week as the center of the whole year. On Palm Sunday, many churches hand out palm branches and walk in procession, then read the long story of Jesus's death, the Passion, so the whole week is felt at once. In Russia and other places where palms don't grow, Orthodox Christians carry pussy willow branches instead. In many places, people walk the Stations of the Cross, stopping to pray at fourteen scenes along the way to the cross. The whole church year, Christians say, turns on this one week.
screen: `HOSANNA: SAVE US, PLEASE.` · `A KING ON A DONKEY.` · `PALMS TO A CROSS IN FIVE DAYS.` · `THE CENTER OF THE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk the road in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a dusty road down a hill into a crowded city. Branches on the ground. The noise. A man on a donkey, moving slowly through all of it, toward whatever is coming. Walk beside him for a while. Notice what he might be feeling. If you pray, you can simply stay with him. If you don't, stay with the picture. Later today, walk one route slowly, to the store, around the block, down a hallway, and remember this road as you go. The bell holds the time.
Palm Sunday and Holy Week. The week from Jesus's entry into Jerusalem to the cross and the empty tomb: the center of the Christian year. Today's word.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY AND HOLY WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the week everything turns. Today, walk one slow route, and let each step be a little remembering. Day one hundred fifteen.

116.title: Maundy Thursday
116.hook: from mandatum, commandment: love one another, and many churches wash feet
116.howItsDone: On Maundy Thursday many churches hold an evening service remembering the Last Supper, often with the washing of feet, and end it by stripping the altar bare; some traditions practice foot washing at other times of the year as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Palm Sunday and Holy Week, and your line: the week everything turns. Did you walk a slow route? Now we're at Thursday of that week, the last night. Day one hundred sixteen.

An upstairs room in Jerusalem. Evening. Supper is on the table, and thirteen people are reclining around it. The roads were dusty, and nobody has washed anyone's feet, which was usually a servant's job. Then the teacher stands up. He takes off his outer robe, ties a towel around his waist, pours water into a basin, and kneels down in front of his friends, one by one. Imagine the silence. When he gets to Peter, Peter can't stand it. In the King James words: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." And Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me." So Peter, being Peter, swings the other way and asks him to wash his hands and his head too. Today's word is the name of that night.
screen: `AN UPSTAIRS ROOM.` → `A TOWEL AND A BASIN.` → `THOU SHALT NEVER WASH MY FEET.`

segments.voice: Maundy. It's an old English form of the Latin mandatum, which means commandment. It comes from what Jesus says later that night, in John's Gospel: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." In Latin, that sentence begins with mandatum, and for centuries it was sung while feet were washed. So the name of the day is really: the day of the commandment. And the commandment has a picture attached. After he washes their feet, Jesus says: "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet." Love here isn't a feeling. It's a towel. It's kneeling. It's doing the job nobody wants. It's the same night as the Last Supper, when Jesus takes bread and wine and tells his friends to do this in remembrance of him. Christians understand that meal in different ways: Catholics and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; many Protestants understand it as a memorial, or as Christ present spiritually. Almost all of them trace communion back to this night. And many churches still wash feet on Maundy Thursday. The pope kneels and washes the feet of twelve people, sometimes prisoners or refugees. In some churches, everyone takes a turn washing someone else's. In Britain, the monarch hands out special coins, Maundy money, to older people each year, a faint echo of the old custom. Then, in many churches, the altar is stripped bare, and the lights go out. The night ends in a garden, with an arrest.
screen: `MANDATUM: COMMANDMENT.` · `LOVE ONE ANOTHER, AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.` · `LOVE IS A TOWEL.` · `A SUPPER, A BASIN, A BARE ALTAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the towel. Settle, and breathe. Picture the room, the basin, the teacher on his knees. Then think of your own home, or work. What's the job nobody wants? The dishes in the sink. The trash. The shared bathroom. The email nobody answers. Pick one. Decide that today, you'll do it for someone else, without mentioning it. If you pray, you can offer it as a way of keeping the commandment. If you don't, just notice what it's like to serve quietly. The bell holds the time.
Maundy. From the Latin mandatum, commandment: love one another. The Thursday before Easter, when many churches wash feet. Today's word.
Your line: love one another. Today, wash someone's dishes, or do their least favorite job, and don't say a word about it. Day one hundred sixteen.
